# Chapter 16 — The Aggregate Picture

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
The synthesis of the preceding fifteen chapters: the tools are individually
strong, the problem is the absence of the substrate that connects them, and
the choice federal agencies face at decommissioning is to accept a less
coherent posture or construct the missing substrate themselves.
:::

## What Has Been Described

The fifteen chapters preceding this one have described, in sequence, the components of the Microsoft identity and governance stack as they actually function: what each tool natively provides, where its native capabilities end, and what questions it cannot answer without custom engineering. The picture that emerges is **not of an inadequate platform**:

* **Entra ID** is a capable, globally available, protocol-compliant identity service.
* **Intune** is a mature unified endpoint-management platform with a deep Windows configuration surface.
* **Azure Arc** extends the Azure control plane to on-premises and multi-cloud workloads in a technically sound manner.
* **Azure Policy** provides enforceable, auditable governance rules for Azure resources.
* **Microsoft Cloud PKI** removes significant operational burden from certificate-infrastructure management.
* **The Defender suite** generates security intelligence of genuine quality within each of its operational domains.

These are not weak tools. They are individually strong. The problem this document has traced is not located in any individual tool.

## The Structural Absence

The problem is located in the absence of the substrate that connects them. Active Directory was imperfect in important ways — its perimeter-based security model was designed for a threat landscape that no longer exists, its privileged-access model creates catastrophic blast radius at the Domain Admin tier, its GPO model is opaque and difficult to audit, and its attack surface is extensively mapped by adversaries who have invested years in techniques exploiting structural properties of Kerberos and NTLM. The case for migrating away from it is clear and well-founded.

> **But Active Directory was coherent.** Every object existed in the same directory. Every governance mechanism shared the same structural model. The OU, the GPO, the DNS record, the certificate template, the computer object, and the user object all related to one another through a single inheritance framework.

An administrator who understood the OU tree understood the policy model, the delegation model, the DNS model, and the certificate-enrollment model simultaneously, because they were all expressions of the same structure. A governance question about any object could be answered by traversing the directory through LDAP. The organizational context of any identity was a property of the directory itself, not a custom attribute maintained through separate integration work.

When that infrastructure is replaced, the individual capabilities arrive but the substrate does not. Each tool brings a different answer to the most fundamental governance question — *what is the organizational structure that defines which policies apply, which administrators have authority, and which resources are in scope?*

| Tool | Its answer to "what is the organization?" |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Entra ID** | The flat tenant and the Administrative Unit. |
| **Intune** | Explicitly assigned groups. |
| **Azure Arc** | The Azure resource group and management group. |
| **Azure Policy** | The management-group hierarchy. |
| **Azure DNS** | The virtual-network link. |
| **Microsoft Cloud PKI** | The Intune certificate profile and device group. |
| **Defender suite** | Object identifiers in separate telemetry streams. |

These answers are not wrong — each is internally coherent within its own tool's model. But they are *different* answers, expressed in different data models, with no native mechanism that translates between them or aggregates them into a single structural view of the organization.

## The Honest Accounting

Federal agencies completing the migration frequently discover this gap not at the planning stage but at the point of **decommissioning**. The migration proceeds tool by tool: identities are synchronized, devices enrolled, servers Arc-connected, DNS partially bridged, Cloud PKI stood up, Defender products deployed. Each step is technically successful; each tool operates within its design parameters. At the moment the decision is made to decommission the last domain controller, the full scope of what is being removed becomes visible — not just an authentication service, a DNS zone, or a policy engine, but the single structural model that gave each of those functions its organizational meaning.

What remains after decommissioning is a collection of individually functional tools that collectively cannot express, without custom engineering, what the on-premises infrastructure expressed as a matter of course: where an identity sits in the organization, what policies flow from that position, who has delegated authority over that segment, and what the blast radius of any change to that segment's governance would be.

> **The choice at decommissioning:** Organizations completing this migration must either accept a governance posture that is structurally less coherent than what they are replacing — explicit rather than inherited policy application, flat rather than hierarchical delegation, organizational context as a custom attribute rather than a structural property — **or** construct the missing substrate themselves: the organizational model, the inheritance logic, the delegation framework, and the cross-tool correlation the platform does not natively provide.

That construction is achievable. It is not trivial. And it is not optional for organizations whose governance obligations require continuous, verifiable, structurally coherent management of identity and policy across the full surface of their IT environment.
